WHEN CALIFORNIA TREATS A BUSINESS AS “DOING BUSINESS” HERE FOR TAX PURPOSES (REV. & TAX. CODE §§ 23101, 23102, 23104, 23114, 23151, 23153, 17941; CORP. CODE § 191; 15 U.S.C. §§ 381, 383; SWART ENTERPRISES, INC. V. FRANCHISE TAX BOARD) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Harbor Lane Holdings, Inc. · Nevada

PURPOSE AND SCOPE — WHEN CALIFORNIA TREATS A BUSINESS AS “DOING BUSINESS” HERE FOR TAX PURPOSES
This information sheet concerns Harbor Lane Holdings, Inc., organized under the law of Nevada, and the separate question California tax law asks about any business, wherever organized: whether it is “doing business” in California within the meaning of Revenue and Taxation Code section 23101. It sets out what the statutes and one published Court of Appeal decision say: the definition of “doing business” in section 23101, subdivision (a); the additional bright-line conditions added for taxable years beginning on or after January 1, 2011, in subdivision (b), the annual indexing of those dollar amounts in subdivision (c), and the attribution of a pass-through entity's sales, property, and payroll to its owners in subdivision (d); the franchise tax imposed on a corporation doing business here by section 23151 and the $800 minimum franchise tax of section 23153, including which corporations that minimum reaches and the first-taxable-year and 15-day rules in sections 23153, subdivision (f)(1), and 23114; the identical “doing business” test carried into the limited liability company annual tax by section 17941; the statutory carve-outs for certain holding companies (section 23102) and short convention or trade show visits (section 23104); the federal limit on a state's power to impose a net income tax on a seller whose only in-state activity is soliciting orders for tangible personal property (Public Law 86-272, 15 U.S.C. §§ 381 and 383); the Fifth District's decision in Swart Enterprises, Inc. v. Franchise Tax Board that an out-of-state corporation passively holding a 0.2 percent interest in a manager-managed California LLC was not doing business here, together with the limits that opinion placed on itself; and the different statutory test — “transact intrastate business” in Corporations Code section 191 — that governs registration with the Secretary of State rather than tax. Whether Harbor Lane Holdings, Inc. is doing business in California in any tax year, what it owes, and what filings apply are questions of fact and of tax administration that this sheet does not determine; naming an entity here does not establish that any rule described below applies to it. This sheet states what the statutes and the court said, and does not advise anyone what to do about a tax year, a filing, an assessment, or a dispute.

THE STATUTORY DEFINITION OF “DOING BUSINESS” AND THE TAX IT TRIGGERS
California's Corporation Tax Law defines “doing business” in a single sentence: it means actively engaging in any transaction for the purpose of financial or pecuniary gain or profit. That definition is not tied to where an entity is organized or whether it has registered with the Secretary of State. The franchise tax itself is imposed by a separate section on every corporation doing business within the limits of this state that is not expressly exempted, and is described in the statute as a tax paid for the privilege of exercising its corporate franchises within this state, measured by net income, or the minimum tax specified in section 23153 if that is greater.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "“Doing business” means actively engaging in any transaction for the purpose of financial or pecuniary gain or profit."
  — Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 23101(a), Corporation Tax Law, definition of “doing business” (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=RTC&sectionNum=23101.)
  "With the exception of banks and financial corporations, every corporation doing business within the limits of this state and not expressly exempted from taxation by the provisions of the Constitution of this state or by this part, shall annually pay to the state, for the privilege of exercising its corporate franchises within this state, a tax according to or measured by its net income, to be computed at the rate of 7.6 percent upon the basis of its net income for the next preceding income year, or if greater, the minimum tax specified in Section 23153."
  — Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 23151(a), Corporation franchise tax imposed on corporations doing business in California (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=RTC&sectionNum=23151.)
  "For any income year beginning on or after January 1, 1997, and before the income year identified in subparagraph (A) of paragraph (1) of subdivision (f), the tax rate shall be 8.84 percent."
  — Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 23151(e), Rate applicable to income years beginning on or after January 1, 1997 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=RTC&sectionNum=23151.)
  Known gap: Subdivision (a) of section 23151 states the tax rate as 7.6 percent, but later subdivisions of the same section supersede that figure; the second citation below quotes subdivision (e), which sets 8.84 percent for income years beginning on or after January 1, 1997, and subdivision (f) provides for a later identified income year, so the rate stated in subdivision (a) is not the operative rate. Banks and financial corporations are excepted from section 23151 and taxed under other sections this sheet does not quote, and the quoted definition in section 23101, subdivision (a), is supplemented for taxable years beginning on or after January 1, 2011, by the conditions in subdivision (b), quoted in the next clause. The Franchise Tax Board's regulation interpreting section 23101 (Cal. Code Regs., tit. 18, § 23101) was not independently fetched for this sheet; it is quoted here only as the Court of Appeal quoted it in Swart Enterprises, in a later clause. Whether a particular activity is “actively engaging in any transaction for the purpose of financial or pecuniary gain or profit” is a fact question this clause does not answer.

THE BRIGHT-LINE CONDITIONS ADDED FOR TAXABLE YEARS BEGINNING ON OR AFTER JANUARY 1, 2011
For taxable years beginning on or after January 1, 2011, the same section states that a taxpayer is doing business in this state if any one of four listed conditions has been satisfied. The first is being organized or commercially domiciled in this state. The other three are dollar-and-percentage thresholds measured against the taxpayer's own totals: California sales exceeding the lesser of $500,000 or 25 percent of total sales; California real and tangible personal property exceeding the lesser of $50,000 or 25 percent of total real and tangible personal property; and California compensation exceeding the lesser of $50,000 or 25 percent of total compensation paid. Each threshold is computed using the assignment rules the statute names — the sales-assignment rules of sections 25135 and 25136, the property rules of sections 25129 to 25131, and the payroll rule of section 25133, each as modified by regulations under section 25137 — and the sales figure includes sales made by an agent or independent contractor of the taxpayer.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "For taxable years beginning on or after January 1, 2011, a taxpayer is doing business in this state for a taxable year if any of the following conditions has been satisfied: (1) The taxpayer is organized or commercially domiciled in this state."
  — Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 23101(b), Conditions establishing that a taxpayer is doing business in California (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=RTC&sectionNum=23101.)
  "Sales, as defined in subdivision (e) or (f) of Section 25120 as applicable for the taxable year, of the taxpayer in this state exceed the lesser of five hundred thousand dollars ($500,000) or 25 percent of the taxpayer’s total sales. For purposes of this paragraph, sales of the taxpayer include sales by an agent or independent contractor of the taxpayer."
  — Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 23101(b)(2), Sales threshold (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=RTC&sectionNum=23101.)
  "The real property and tangible personal property of the taxpayer in this state exceed the lesser of fifty thousand dollars ($50,000) or 25 percent of the taxpayer’s total real property and tangible personal property."
  — Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 23101(b)(3), Property threshold (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=RTC&sectionNum=23101.)
  "The amount paid in this state by the taxpayer for compensation, as defined in subdivision (c) of Section 25120, exceeds the lesser of fifty thousand dollars ($50,000) or 25 percent of the total compensation paid by the taxpayer."
  — Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 23101(b)(4), Compensation threshold (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=RTC&sectionNum=23101.)
  Known gap: The dollar figures quoted here are the amounts as enacted; subdivision (c) of the same section directs the Franchise Tax Board to revise them annually for inflation, so the figures in force for a given taxable year are higher than the enacted amounts quoted below (see the following clause). This clause does not quote the cross-referenced assignment rules in sections 25120, 25129 through 25137, which control how sales, property, and payroll are assigned to California and can change the result. These conditions are additional to, not a replacement for, the definition in subdivision (a); a taxpayer below every threshold may still be doing business under subdivision (a). Whether any of these conditions is satisfied for a given entity and year is a factual computation this sheet does not perform.

ANNUAL INDEXING OF THE THRESHOLDS, AND ATTRIBUTION OF A PASS-THROUGH ENTITY'S SALES, PROPERTY, AND PAYROLL
Two further subdivisions of the same section change how the thresholds are applied. First, the statute directs the Franchise Tax Board to revise the sales, property, and compensation amounts annually under the personal income tax inflation-adjustment provision, applied by substituting 2012 for 1988 — so the operative figures for a given taxable year are the indexed figures the Board publishes, not the enacted $500,000 and $50,000 amounts. Second, the statute provides that a taxpayer's sales, property, and payroll include the taxpayer's pro rata or distributive share of pass-through entities, and defines “pass-through entities” for that purpose as a partnership or an “S” corporation. A limited liability company classified as a partnership for tax purposes is treated as a partnership under the Corporation Tax Law's classification rules, which the Court of Appeal described in the decision quoted later in this sheet.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "(1) The Franchise Tax Board shall annually revise the amounts in paragraphs (2), (3), and (4) of subdivision (b) in accordance with subdivision (h) of Section 17041. (2) For purposes of the adjustment required by paragraph (1), subdivision (h) of Section 17041 shall be applied by substituting “2012” in lieu of “1988.”"
  — Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 23101(c), Annual revision of the threshold amounts (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=RTC&sectionNum=23101.)
  "The sales, property, and payroll of the taxpayer include the taxpayer’s pro rata or distributive share of pass-through entities. For purposes of this subdivision, “pass-through entities” means a partnership or an “S” corporation."
  — Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 23101(d), Inclusion of a pro rata or distributive share of pass-through entities (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=RTC&sectionNum=23101.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes the indexing instruction but not the inflation-adjustment mechanics of Revenue and Taxation Code section 17041, subdivision (h), which it incorporates, and it does not state the indexed dollar figures for any particular year; those are published by the Franchise Tax Board and change annually, so any figure stated here would go stale. The statutory definition of “pass-through entities” quoted below names a partnership or an “S” corporation and does not itself name limited liability companies; the treatment of an LLC turns on its classification under the entity-classification rules (Rev. & Tax. Code § 23038, subd. (b)(2)(B)) and the federal check-the-box regulations, which this clause does not quote. Whether a particular owner's distributive share pushes it over a threshold is a computation this sheet does not perform.

THE $800 MINIMUM FRANCHISE TAX REACHES CORPORATIONS BY THREE SEPARATE ROUTES
The minimum franchise tax is not limited to California-formed corporations. The statute makes the minimum tax applicable, unless expressly exempted, to every corporation incorporated under the laws of this state, every corporation qualified to transact intrastate business here under the foreign-qualification chapter of the Corporations Code, and every corporation that is doing business in this state — three independent routes, so a corporation formed elsewhere and never registered here is reached by the third if it is doing business here. The liability runs from the earlier of the date of incorporation, qualification, or commencing to do business within this state, until the effective date of dissolution or withdrawal or, if later, the date the corporation ceases to do business within the limits of this state. The amount is $800.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "Every corporation described in subdivision (b) shall be subject to the minimum franchise tax specified in subdivision (d) from the earlier of the date of incorporation, qualification, or commencing to do business within this state, until the effective date of dissolution or withdrawal as provided in Section 23331 or, if later, the date the corporation ceases to do business within the limits of this state."
  — Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 23153(a), Period for which the minimum franchise tax applies (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=RTC&sectionNum=23153.)
  "Unless expressly exempted by this part or the California Constitution, subdivision (a) shall apply to each of the following: (1) Every corporation that is incorporated under the laws of this state. (2) Every corporation that is qualified to transact intrastate business in this state pursuant to Chapter 21 (commencing with Section 2100) of Division 1 of Title 1 of the Corporations Code. (3) Every corporation that is doing business in this state."
  — Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 23153(b), Corporations to which the minimum franchise tax applies (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=RTC&sectionNum=23153.)
  "corporations subject to the minimum franchise tax shall pay annually to the state a minimum franchise tax of eight hundred dollars ($800)."
  — Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 23153(d)(1), Amount of the minimum franchise tax (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=RTC&sectionNum=23153.)
  Known gap: The quoted subdivision (d)(1) begins with exceptions this clause's quote omits — it is expressly subject to paragraph (2) of the same subdivision and to three other sections (§§ 23151, subd. (f)(1), 23181, subd. (f)(1), and 23183, subd. (c)(1)) — and paragraph (2) sets a $25 minimum for certain inactive gold-mining and quicksilver-mining corporations. Subdivision (c) of the same section excludes credit unions and certain certificated nonprofit cooperative associations, and other exemptions appear elsewhere in the part (for example, exempt organizations under § 23701). This clause does not address banks or financial corporations, which are taxed under separate sections, or the first-year and short-period rules quoted in the next clause. It also does not state what any specific corporation owes for any year.

THE FIRST-TAXABLE-YEAR EXEMPTION AND THE 15-DAY RULE
Two statutory rules narrow the minimum tax at the beginning of a corporation's life. The first exempts a corporation from the minimum franchise tax for its first taxable year, but by its terms it reaches a corporation that incorporates or qualifies to do business in this state on or after January 1, 2000 — it is keyed to the act of incorporating or qualifying, not to commencing to do business. The second states that a corporation is not subject to the taxes imposed by the franchise tax chapter if it did no business in this state during the taxable year and the taxable year was 15 days or less, and adds that such a period is not counted as a taxable year for purposes of the first-year rule.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "Notwithstanding subdivision (a), every corporation that incorporates or qualifies to do business in this state on or after January 1, 2000, shall not be subject to the minimum franchise tax for its first taxable year."
  — Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 23153(f)(1), First taxable year of a corporation that incorporates or qualifies on or after January 1, 2000 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=RTC&sectionNum=23153.)
  "(a) A corporation shall not be subject to the taxes imposed by this chapter if the corporation did no business in this state during the taxable year and the taxable year was 15 days or less. (b) The period of time for which a corporation is not subject to taxes imposed by this chapter as provided in subdivision (a) may not be considered a taxable year for purposes of subdivision (e) or paragraph (1) of subdivision (f) of Section 23153."
  — Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 23114, Taxable year of 15 days or less with no business done in this state (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=RTC&sectionNum=23114.)
  Known gap: The first-year exemption quoted here does not apply to every entity: paragraph (2) of the same subdivision excludes limited partnerships, limited liability companies, limited liability partnerships, charitable organizations, regulated investment companies, real estate investment trusts, real estate mortgage investment conduits, and qualified subchapter S subsidiaries, and this clause does not quote that list. The 15-day rule requires both conditions — no business done in this state and a taxable year of 15 days or less — and section 23113 separately provides that the tax attaches whether the taxable year is twelve months or less. Whether a particular corporation's first taxable year or short period meets these conditions is a factual question this sheet does not resolve.

THE SAME DEFINITION CARRIES INTO THE LLC ANNUAL TAX — AND A SECOND, FILING-BASED TRIGGER
The annual tax on a limited liability company uses the same definition. The statute imposes the tax on a limited liability company doing business in this state “as defined in Section 23101,” in an amount equal to the applicable amount specified in section 23153, subdivision (d) — the same figure as the corporate minimum franchise tax. A second subdivision adds an independent, filing-based trigger: in addition to an LLC that is doing business here, an LLC owes the same annual tax if articles of organization have been accepted, or a certificate of registration has been issued, by the office of the Secretary of State, and that obligation continues for each taxable year, or part of one, until a certificate of cancellation of registration or of articles of organization is filed with the Secretary of State. So an LLC can owe the tax either by doing business here or by having a filing on record here.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "Except as provided in subdivision (g), for each taxable year beginning on or after January 1, 1997, a limited liability company doing business in this state (as defined in Section 23101) shall pay annually to this state a tax for the privilege of doing business in this state in an amount equal to the applicable amount specified in subdivision (d) of Section 23153 for the taxable year."
  — Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 17941(a), Annual tax on a limited liability company doing business in California (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=RTC&sectionNum=17941.)
  "In addition to any limited liability company that is doing business in this state and is therefore subject to the tax imposed by subdivision (a), for each taxable year beginning on or after January 1, 1997, a limited liability company shall pay annually the tax prescribed in subdivision (a) if articles of organization have been accepted, or a certificate of registration has been issued, by the office of the Secretary of State. The tax shall be paid for each taxable year, or part thereof, until a certificate of cancellation of registration or of articles of organization is filed on behalf of the limited liability company with the office of the Secretary of State."
  — Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 17941(b)(1), Filing-based trigger for the LLC annual tax (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=RTC&sectionNum=17941.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes subdivisions (a) and (b)(1) of section 17941 only. It does not quote subdivision (g) (referenced in the opening exception of subdivision (a)), subdivision (d)'s definition of “limited liability company” for this section, subdivision (e), or the due-date rule in subdivision (c), and it does not address the separate, income-based LLC fee imposed by section 17942, which this corpus's California LLC Annual Fee sheet covers. Parallel annual taxes on limited partnerships and registered limited liability partnerships appear in sections 17935 and 17948 and are not quoted here. The consequences of nonpayment, and any exemption, are outside this clause.

TWO STATUTORY CARVE-OUTS: PASSIVE STOCK-AND-BOND HOLDING COMPANIES AND SHORT TRADE SHOW VISITS
The same article contains two narrow statements that specified activity is not doing business. One addresses a holding company: a corporation holding or organized to hold stock or bonds of other corporations, not trading in the securities it holds, and engaging in no activities other than receiving and disbursing dividends and bond interest, is not a corporation doing business in this state for purposes of the franchise tax chapter. The other addresses visitors: a corporation not incorporated under California law whose sole activity here is convention and trade show activities, as described in the federal tax provision the statute names, for seven or fewer calendar days in the taxable year, and that does not derive more than $10,000 of gross income reportable to this state from those activities that year, is not a corporation doing business in this state.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "Any corporation holding or organized to hold stock or bonds of any other corporation or corporations, and not trading in stock or bonds or other securities held, and engaging in no activities other than the receipt and disbursement of dividends from stock or interest from bonds, is not a corporation doing business in this State for the purposes of this chapter."
  — Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 23102, Certain holding companies are not doing business in California (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=RTC&sectionNum=23102.)
  "For purposes of this part only, any corporation that is not incorporated under the laws of this state and whose sole activity in this state is engaging in convention and trade show activities, as described in Section 513(d)(3)(A) of the Internal Revenue Code, for seven or fewer calendar days, or any portion thereof, during the taxable year and that does not derive more than ten thousand dollars ($10,000) of gross income reportable to this state from those activities during that taxable year is not a corporation doing business in this state."
  — Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 23104(a), Convention and trade show activities of seven or fewer days (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=RTC&sectionNum=23104.)
  Known gap: Both carve-outs are written in absolute terms — “engaging in no activities other than” receipt and disbursement of dividends and interest, and “whose sole activity in this state” is short-duration convention and trade show activity — so any additional California activity takes an entity outside them; this clause does not decide whether a given company's activities stay inside those lines. The trade show provision incorporates Internal Revenue Code section 513(d)(3)(A)'s description of convention and trade show activities, which this clause does not quote, and its gross-income test is measured across a commonly controlled group under section 25105. A separate section, 23101.5, allows the Franchise Tax Board to determine that a corporation whose only California activities are certain purchasing activities or employees attending school is not doing business, on petition and subject to employee-count limits; that determination procedure is not quoted here. The holding-company provision, enacted in this form in 1951, uses the capitalized phrase “this State,” which is reproduced as it appears in the code.

A FEDERAL LIMIT ON STATE NET INCOME TAXES: PUBLIC LAW 86-272
A federal statute enacted in 1959 limits every state's power to impose a net income tax in one specific situation. No state may impose a net income tax on income derived within the state from interstate commerce if the only business activities within the state by or on behalf of the person are the solicitation of orders for sales of tangible personal property that are sent outside the state for approval or rejection and, if approved, filled by shipment or delivery from a point outside the state, or the solicitation of such orders in the name of or for the benefit of a prospective customer. The same statute says that protection does not apply to a corporation incorporated under the laws of the taxing state or to an individual domiciled in or a resident of that state, and that a person is not treated as engaged in business activities in a state merely because of sales or solicitation of orders there carried on by independent contractors. A separate section of the same federal chapter defines “net income tax” as any tax imposed on, or measured by, net income.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "No State, or political subdivision thereof, shall have power to impose, for any taxable year ending after September 14, 1959, a net income tax on the income derived within such State by any person from interstate commerce if the only business activities within such State by or on behalf of such person during such taxable year are either, or both, of the following: (1) the solicitation of orders by such person, or his representative, in such State for sales of tangible personal property, which orders are sent outside the State for approval or rejection, and, if approved, are filled by shipment or delivery from a point outside the State; and (2) the solicitation of orders by such person, or his representative, in such State in the name of or for the benefit of a prospective customer of such person, if orders by such customer to such person to enable such customer to fill orders resulting from such solicitation are orders described in paragraph (1)."
  — 15 U.S.C. § 381(a), Public Law 86-272, minimum standards for state net income taxation (https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title15-section381&num=0&edition=prelim)
  "The provisions of subsection (a) shall not apply to the imposition of a net income tax by any State, or political subdivision thereof, with respect to— (1) any corporation which is incorporated under the laws of such State; or (2) any individual who, under the laws of such State, is domiciled in, or a resident of, such State."
  — 15 U.S.C. § 381(b), Exclusion of corporations incorporated in, and individuals resident in, the taxing state (https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title15-section381&num=0&edition=prelim)
  "For purposes of this chapter, the term "net income tax" means any tax imposed on, or measured by, net income."
  — 15 U.S.C. § 383, Definition of “net income tax” (https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title15-section383&num=0&edition=prelim)
  Known gap: This federal statute is quoted here as a limit on a state's power to impose a net income tax; it is limited on its face to sales of tangible personal property and to solicitation, and it says nothing about taxes that are not net income taxes, about services, intangibles, or digital products, or about state registration and filing requirements. Whether California's $800 minimum franchise tax, or any other specific levy, is a “net income tax” within the federal definition is a legal question this clause does not answer and no source quoted in this sheet decides. The independent-contractor provision in subdivision (c) has its own qualifications, including a proviso about maintaining an office, which this clause does not quote, and subdivision (d) defines “independent contractor” and “representative.” The Franchise Tax Board's published interpretations of this statute, and the Multistate Tax Commission's statement on internet activities, are administrative materials not quoted here. These sections were fetched from two independent government sources, the Office of the Law Revision Counsel's United States Code website and the Government Publishing Office's govinfo text of the same sections; the two agree word for word except that the Law Revision Counsel's page renders the dash in subsection (b)'s phrase “with respect to—” as a plain hyphen, and the quotation below follows the Government Publishing Office's typography.

SWART ENTERPRISES: A PASSIVE 0.2 PERCENT MEMBER OF A MANAGER-MANAGED CALIFORNIA LLC WAS NOT DOING BUSINESS HERE
In 2017 the Fifth District Court of Appeal decided whether the franchise tax reached an out-of-state corporation whose only connection with California was a 0.2 percent ownership interest in a manager-managed California limited liability company investment fund. The corporation was an Iowa farming company with no California property, employees, sales, or registration; it had invested $50,000 in the fund. The court held that passively holding that interest, with no right of control over the business affairs of the LLC, is not “doing business” in California within the meaning of section 23101, comparing the investor to a shareholder who merely receives dividends and interest, and treating its position as akin to that of a limited partner rather than a general partner. The court rejected the argument that the LLC's election to be taxed as a partnership converted its members into general partners whose share of the LLC's activity could be imputed to them, and it disagreed with the analysis of the Franchise Tax Board's own legal ruling taking the contrary position.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "We conclude passively holding a 0.2 percent ownership interest, with no right of control over the business affairs of the LLC, does not constitute “doing business” in California within the meaning of section 23101."
  — Swart Enterprises, Inc. v. Franchise Tax Board, (2017) 7 Cal.App.5th 497, 500 (slip opn., p. 2) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/4338268/swart-enterprises-inc-v-franchise-tax-board/)
  "Here, the $800 minimum franchise tax was imposed upon Swart several years after Swart made its investment and became a member of Cypress LLC. We are not persuaded such an investment, without more, is sufficient to conclude Swart was doing business in California. Like a shareholder’s receipt of dividends and interest, Swart merely passively held onto its investment in the tax year the franchise tax was imposed."
  — Swart Enterprises, Inc. v. Franchise Tax Board, (2017) 7 Cal.App.5th 497, 504 (slip opn., pp. 6-7) (https://storage.courtlistener.com/pdf/2017/01/12/swart_enterprises_v._franchise_tax_bd..pdf)
  "Under these circumstances, Swart’s interest in Cypress LLC was akin to that of a limited partner, and it cannot be deemed to be “doing business” in California by virtue of the fact Cypress LLC was “doing business” in California."
  — Swart Enterprises, Inc. v. Franchise Tax Board, (2017) 7 Cal.App.5th 497, 511 (slip opn., p. 15) (https://storage.courtlistener.com/pdf/2017/01/12/swart_enterprises_v._franchise_tax_bd..pdf)
  "We conclude Swart was not doing business in California based solely on its minority ownership interest in Cypress LLC."
  — Swart Enterprises, Inc. v. Franchise Tax Board, (2017) 7 Cal.App.5th 497, 513 (slip opn., p. 18) (https://storage.courtlistener.com/pdf/2017/01/12/swart_enterprises_v._franchise_tax_bd..pdf)
  Known gap: The court's reasoning rested on the facts before it: an ownership interest of 0.2 percent, a manager-managed fund whose operating agreement barred the non-managing member from participating in management and control, a manager designated two years before this member invested, and no contention that the member actually participated in management. It is a single published Court of Appeal decision, not a Supreme Court decision, and the tax year at issue preceded the bright-line conditions of section 23101, subdivision (b) — see the following clause, which quotes the court's own footnote on that point. The quotations below are taken word for word from the court's certified-for-publication slip opinion PDF (filed January 12, 2017), and each passage was located a second time in the Official Reports text served by CourtListener as HTML, fetched twice with different browser header sets; that second text is an optical-character-recognition transcription that corrupts individual words in these same passages — it renders “Like a shareholder’s” as “Fike a shareholder’s” and “Cypress LLC” as “Cypress FFC” — so where the two differ this sheet follows the slip opinion and the quoted strings match it exactly. The holding sentence was additionally confirmed through CourtListener's public search index as an exact phrase restricted to this opinion's cluster. The Franchise Tax Board legal ruling and the State Board of Equalization decisions the court discusses are administrative materials that were not independently fetched for this sheet.

WHAT THE SWART OPINION SAID ABOUT ITS OWN LIMITS
The opinion marks its own boundaries in three places. In a footnote, the court noted that the bright-line bases added for taxable years beginning on or after January 1, 2011 — being organized or commercially domiciled in California, or exceeding the California sales, property, or payroll amounts — did not apply to the taxpayer before it, because the franchise tax at issue was imposed for a tax year ending June 30, 2010. In a second footnote, after holding that a member of a manager-managed LLC whose operating agreement expressly prohibited it from participating in management had no right of control, the court said it could envision circumstances where the parties' conduct might show a member's participation in control despite the operating agreement, but that such circumstances were not present. And the court expressly declined to reach the taxpayer's constitutional challenge to the tax, because deciding it was not necessary to the disposition.

A DIFFERENT STATUTE, A DIFFERENT TEST: “TRANSACTING INTRASTATE BUSINESS” FOR SECRETARY OF STATE REGISTRATION
California uses a different phrase, in a different code, for the question whether an out-of-state entity must register with the Secretary of State. For that chapter, “transact intrastate business” means entering into repeated and successive transactions of its business in this state, other than interstate or foreign commerce. The same section states that a foreign corporation is not considered to be transacting intrastate business merely because a subsidiary transacts intrastate business, or merely because of its status as a shareholder of a domestic or foreign corporation, a limited partner of a domestic or foreign limited partnership, or a member or manager of a domestic or foreign limited liability company. The two tests are separate: registration status is one of the three independent routes by which the minimum franchise tax reaches a corporation, so a corporation that registers here is subject to that tax whether or not it is doing business, and a corporation that never registers may still be doing business for tax purposes.

It sets out what the statutes and one published Court of Appeal decision say: the definition of “doing business” in section 23101, subdivision (a); the additional bright-line conditions added for taxable years beginning on or after January 1, 2011, in subdivision (b), the annual indexing of those dollar amounts in subdivision (c), and the attribution of a pass-through entity's sales, property, and payroll to its owners in subdivision (d); the franchise tax imposed on a corporation doing business here by section 23151 and the $800 minimum franchise tax of section 23153, including which corporations that minimum reaches and the first-taxable-year and 15-day rules in sections 23153, subdivision (f)(1), and 23114; the identical “doing business” test carried into the limited liability company annual tax by section 17941; the statutory carve-outs for certain holding companies (section 23102) and short convention or trade show visits (section 23104); the federal limit on a state's power to impose a net income tax on a seller whose only in-state activity is soliciting orders for tangible personal property (Public Law 86-272, 15 U.S.C. §§ 381 and 383); the Fifth District's decision in Swart Enterprises, Inc. v. Franchise Tax Board that an out-of-state corporation passively holding a 0.2 percent interest in a manager-managed California LLC was not doing business here, together with the limits that opinion placed on itself; and the different statutory test — “transact intrastate business” in Corporations Code section 191 — that governs registration with the Secretary of State rather than tax. Whether Harbor Lane Holdings, Inc. is doing business in California in any tax year, what it owes, and what filings apply are questions of fact and of tax administration that this sheet does not determine; naming an entity here does not establish that any rule described below applies to it. This sheet states what the statutes and the court said, and does not advise anyone what to do about a tax year, a filing, an assessment, or a dispute.

California's Corporation Tax Law defines “doing business” in a single sentence: it means actively engaging in any transaction for the purpose of financial or pecuniary gain or profit. That definition is not tied to where an entity is organized or whether it has registered with the Secretary of State. The franchise tax itself is imposed by a separate section on every corporation doing business within the limits of this state that is not expressly exempted, and is described in the statute as a tax paid for the privilege of exercising its corporate franchises within this state, measured by net income, or the minimum tax specified in section 23153 if that is greater.

expectedJSON.body: For taxable years beginning on or after January 1, 2011, the same section states that a taxpayer is doing business in this state if any one of four listed conditions has been satisfied. The first is being organized or commercially domiciled in this state. The other three are dollar-and-percentage thresholds measured against the taxpayer's own totals: California sales exceeding the lesser of $500,000 or 25 percent of total sales; California real and tangible personal property exceeding the lesser of $50,000 or 25 percent of total real and tangible personal property; and California compensation exceeding the lesser of $50,000 or 25 percent of total compensation paid. Each threshold is computed using the assignment rules the statute names — the sales-assignment rules of sections 25135 and 25136, the property rules of sections 25129 to 25131, and the payroll rule of section 25133, each as modified by regulations under section 25137 — and the sales figure includes sales made by an agent or independent contractor of the taxpayer.

citations.quote: Sales, as defined in subdivision (e) or (f) of Section 25120 as applicable for the taxable year, of the taxpayer in this state exceed the lesser of five hundred thousand dollars ($500,000) or 25 percent of the taxpayer’s total sales. For purposes of this paragraph, sales of the taxpayer include sales by an agent or independent contractor of the taxpayer.

citations.cite: Compensation threshold

The liability runs from the earlier of the date of incorporation, qualification, or commencing to do business within this state, until the effective date of dissolution or withdrawal or, if later, the date the corporation ceases to do business within the limits of this state. expectedJSON.body: In 2017 the Fifth District Court of Appeal decided whether the franchise tax reached an out-of-state corporation whose only connection with California was a 0.2 percent ownership interest in a manager-managed California limited liability company investment fund. The corporation was an Iowa farming company with no California property, employees, sales, or registration; it had invested $50,000 in the fund. The court held that passively holding that interest, with no right of control over the business affairs of the LLC, is not “doing business” in California within the meaning of section 23101, comparing the investor to a shareholder who merely receives dividends and interest, and treating its position as akin to that of a limited partner rather than a general partner. The court rejected the argument that the LLC's election to be taxed as a partnership converted its members into general partners whose share of the LLC's activity could be imputed to them, and it disagreed with the analysis of the Franchise Tax Board's own legal ruling taking the contrary position.

citations.quote: We conclude Swart was not doing business in California based solely on its minority ownership interest in Cypress LLC.

expectedJSON.gap: The court's reasoning rested on the facts before it: an ownership interest of 0.2 percent, a manager-managed fund whose operating agreement barred the non-managing member from participating in management and control, a manager designated two years before this member invested, and no contention that the member actually participated in management. It is a single published Court of Appeal decision, not a Supreme Court decision, and the tax year at issue preceded the bright-line conditions of section 23101, subdivision (b) — see the following clause, which quotes the court's own footnote on that point. The quotations below are taken word for word from the court's certified-for-publication slip opinion PDF (filed January 12, 2017), and each passage was located a second time in the Official Reports text served by CourtListener as HTML, fetched twice with different browser header sets; that second text is an optical-character-recognition transcription that corrupts individual words in these same passages — it renders “Like a shareholder’s” as “Fike a shareholder’s” and “Cypress LLC” as “Cypress FFC” — so where the two differ this sheet follows the slip opinion and the quoted strings match it exactly. The holding sentence was additionally confirmed through CourtListener's public search index as an exact phrase restricted to this opinion's cluster. The Franchise Tax Board legal ruling and the State Board of Equalization decisions the court discusses are administrative materials that were not independently fetched for this sheet.

expectedJSON.body: The opinion marks its own boundaries in three places. In a footnote, the court noted that the bright-line bases added for taxable years beginning on or after January 1, 2011 — being organized or commercially domiciled in California, or exceeding the California sales, property, or payroll amounts — did not apply to the taxpayer before it, because the franchise tax at issue was imposed for a tax year ending June 30, 2010. In a second footnote, after holding that a member of a manager-managed LLC whose operating agreement expressly prohibited it from participating in management had no right of control, the court said it could envision circumstances where the parties' conduct might show a member's participation in control despite the operating agreement, but that such circumstances were not present. And the court expressly declined to reach the taxpayer's constitutional challenge to the tax, because deciding it was not necessary to the disposition.

citations.case: Swart Enterprises, Inc. v. Franchise Tax Board
citations.cite: (2017) 7 Cal.App.5th 497, 503, fn. 2 (slip opn., p. 6, fn. 2)
citations.quote: For tax years beginning on or after January 1, 2011, a taxpayer is also “doing business” in California if the taxpayer is organized or commercially domiciled in California, or a taxpayer’s California sales, property, or payroll exceed the amounts applicable under subdivision (b)(1) of section 23101. Because the franchise tax was imposed for Swart’s tax year ending June 30, 2010, these new bases for “doing business” do not apply to Swart.

citations.quote: Although we can envision circumstances where the parties’ conduct may evince an LLC member’s participation in the control of the LLC, notwithstanding restrictions set forth in the operating agreement, such circumstances are not present here.

citations.quote: Bearing in mind that a reviewing court should consider a constitutional question only where essential to the disposition of a case, we do not reach Swart’s challenge to the franchise tax on constitutional grounds

expectedJSON.gap: These limits are quoted from the opinion itself and are not a complete list of questions it left open. The three quotations are taken from the slip opinion PDF and were located again in the Official Reports text served by CourtListener; that second text is an optical-character-recognition transcription that corrupts individual words in these passages (for example, it renders “Swart’s tax year ending June 30, 2010” as “Swait’s”), so the quoted strings follow the slip opinion. The third quotation stops at “on constitutional grounds” because the sentence continues across a page break in the slip opinion, where a footnote intervenes; the remainder of that sentence reads “as it was not necessary to the disposition of this matter.” The decision does not address a member with a larger interest, a member-managed LLC, a member who actually participates in management, an owner whose distributive share exceeds the post-2011 thresholds now attributed by section 23101, subdivision (d), or any entity other than an out-of-state corporation holding an LLC interest. It also does not decide the constitutional limits on California's franchise tax. The Franchise Tax Board's Legal Ruling No. 2014-01, which the court disagreed with, is an administrative position that this sheet neither quotes in full nor evaluates; whether and how the Board has since applied it is outside this sheet.

expectedJSON.body: California uses a different phrase, in a different code, for the question whether an out-of-state entity must register with the Secretary of State. For that chapter, “transact intrastate business” means entering into repeated and successive transactions of its business in this state, other than interstate or foreign commerce. The same section states that a foreign corporation is not considered to be transacting intrastate business merely because a subsidiary transacts intrastate business, or merely because of its status as a shareholder of a domestic or foreign corporation, a limited partner of a domestic or foreign limited partnership, or a member or manager of a domestic or foreign limited liability company. The two tests are separate: registration status is one of the three independent routes by which the minimum franchise tax reaches a corporation, so a corporation that registers here is subject to that tax whether or not it is doing business, and a corporation that never registers may still be doing business for tax purposes.

citations.cite: Definition of “transact intrastate business” for the foreign-qualification chapter
citations.quote: For the purposes of Chapter 21 (commencing with Section 2100), “transact intrastate business” means entering into repeated and successive transactions of its business in this state, other than interstate or foreign commerce.

citations.cite: Ownership statuses that do not by themselves constitute transacting intrastate business
citations.quote: A foreign corporation shall not be considered to be transacting intrastate business merely because its subsidiary transacts intrastate business or merely because of its status as any one or more of the following: (1) A shareholder of a domestic corporation. (2) A shareholder of a foreign corporation transacting intrastate business. (3) A limited partner of a domestic limited partnership. (4) A limited partner of a foreign limited partnership transacting intrastate business. (5) A member or manager of a domestic limited liability company. (6) A member or manager of a foreign limited liability company transacting intrastate business.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause quotes subdivisions (a) and (b) of Corporations Code section 191. It does not quote subdivision (c)'s list of activities that do not by themselves constitute transacting intrastate business (litigation, internal-affairs meetings, bank accounts, transfer agencies, sales through independent contractors, orders requiring out-of-state acceptance, security interests, and isolated transactions completed within 180 days), or the remaining subdivisions, and the registration requirements and penalties themselves appear in Corporations Code sections 2100 through 2115 and 17708.01 through 17708.07, which this corpus's Foreign LLC/Corporation Qualification sheet covers. This clause states that the tax and registration tests are worded differently and are found in different statutes; it does not decide how either applies to a particular business, and no source quoted here holds that satisfying one test settles the other.
